name: Ruy López
summary: The Ruy López (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5) pressures Black’s knight and remains the most respected of the Open Games.
intro: The Ruy López, or Spanish Opening, is reached after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5. By pinning attention on the c6-knight that defends e5, White poses long-term positional questions that have made it a mainstay at every level for over four hundred years.

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The Ruy López begins 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5, developing the bishop with the idea of pressuring the c6-knight that defends the e5-pawn. Although the bishop does not win the pawn outright, its presence creates lasting positional questions for Black, especially the recurring threat to trade on c6 and damage the black pawn structure. The result is one of the deepest and most respected openings in all of chess, prized for its blend of subtle manoeuvring and long-term strategic tension.

A defining feature is the slow, manoeuvring character of the main lines. White often plays c3 and d4 to build a broad pawn centre, and a hallmark of the opening is the knight journey Nb1-d2-f1-g3 (or e3), redeploying the queen's knight toward the kingside. Both sides typically castle short and spend considerable energy jockeying for the best piece placement before the position opens.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: Black's most popular response is 3...a6, the Morphy Defence, questioning the bishop at once. After 4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O, Black chooses between the solid Closed lines with ...Be7 and ...b5, and the sharp Open Variation with 5...Nxe4. The Marshall Attack, in which Black sacrifices a pawn for a powerful kingside initiative, is one of the most analysed gambits in the Ruy López and forces White to prepare a specific antidote.

Black also has many independent third moves. The Berlin Defence (3...Nf6) leads to a famous endgame where Black accepts doubled pawns and the loss of castling in return for a resilient, resourceful structure. Other well-known systems include the Classical Defence (3...Bc5), the Schliemann (3...f5), and the Steinitz setups with ...d6, each giving the opening its own distinct flavour.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The opening takes its name from Ruy López de Segura, a sixteenth-century Spanish priest who analysed it in one of the earliest printed chess treatises, and it is still widely called the Spanish Game. It became a cornerstone of classical opening theory in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries and has been employed by essentially every World Champion. Its enduring reputation as a testing ground for positional understanding has earned it the nickname the Spanish Torture, reflecting the slow, grinding pressure White can generate.

keyIdeas: 3.Bb5 pins pressure onto the c6-knight, indirectly targeting the e5-pawn.
White builds a broad centre with c3 and d4 and manoeuvres for the long term.
The knight route Nb1-d2-f1-g3 redeploys the queen's knight toward the kingside.
The threat to trade on c6 and damage Black's pawns is a recurring positional theme.
Both sides castle short and jockey for piece placement before the centre opens.
Rich menu of defences: Morphy, Berlin, Marshall, Classical, and Schliemann.

white: Prepare c3 and d4 to establish a strong central pawn duo.
Reroute the b1-knight via d2-f1-g3 to support a kingside build-up.
Consider Bxc6 at the right moment to inflict doubled pawns on Black.
Maintain the central tension and slowly increase pressure across the board.
Prepare a sound antidote against the Marshall Attack if allowing ...O-O lines.
black: Challenge the bishop with 3...a6, gaining the option to expand with ...b5.
Complete development with ...Be7, ...O-O, and reroute the knight to safety.
Seek the freeing ...d5 break, as in the Marshall and Open Variations.
Choose the Berlin for a solid endgame-oriented, low-risk structure.
Generate counterplay on the queenside or against White's centre when it advances.
